# Webhook Compatibility Migration Workflow

Old links still lead to this record, so it has not been cleaned up into a single page of conclusions in the current style. The earliest checking method was straightforward: work backward from a notification that had already been delivered, and if the receiver had content, mark both the label text and request timeouts as normal. It was useful at the time for answering "was the webhook never sent at all", and it did let people quickly find their way back to the sending entry point; but it is no longer suitable as a basis for compatibility sign-off.

The entry point identified in the old record is `src/robusta/core/sinks/webhook/webhook_sink.py`. The file contains `import textwrap`, `from typing import List`, and `import requests`, and the reporting side directly imports `HeaderBlock`, `JsonBlock`, `KubernetesDiffBlock`, `ListBlock`, `MarkdownBlock`. Therefore, when tracing back, first treat it as a reference point near where webhook payloads are formed and sent, rather than merely a forwarding point for a fixed string.

The troubleshooting approach at the time followed names such as webhook, url, finding, and `requests.post` to this file, then put every observation into the "sending succeeded or failed" category. That had one clear consequence: screenshots from the receiver became the only indirect evidence of whether labels were present; when a request took a long time, no parameters or return status were retained from that run, leaving only "that notification was rather slow".

The differences between the old path and the records that were later separated are as follows:

```text
Old path
finding ──> Assemble message ──> Send ──> Receiver has content
                              └── Old record: Normal

Separated records
finding ──> Label set ──> Display text ──> Receiver display

Request parameters ──> Wait / Return status ──> Retain separately
```

The two downstream lines in the diagram can come from the same trigger, but do not let one stand in for the other when drawing conclusions anymore. A label line being displayed by the receiver does not mean that the request used verifiable wait settings; a request eventually completing does not mean that the display in Slack-compatible preserved the finding's labels.

## What to Migrate out of the Old Checks First

Not all of the old checks are invalid. Retaining the return status after sending still helps determine whether this webhook has completed; it is also still worth keeping when restoring the old method. The part being migrated out is the interpretation of this result as "both labels and timeouts have been checked".

When checking labels, leave the sending step unchanged for now. After triggering a notification with a finding, retain three things separately: the label set actually present in the finding, the relevant fragment that went into the webhook display text, and the line ultimately displayed by the receiver. If any of the three is missing, state which part is missing, rather than using a screenshot or return status to infer the intermediate content.

This does not require organizing the material in the same format every time. When a legacy caller can only provide a screenshot, the screenshot is still useful because it shows that the receiver displayed a notification at some point; just also note that the pre-send text cannot be found. If all you have is a payload fragment and the receiver's result cannot be viewed, do not say that compatibility is complete simply because the text looks reasonable. Earlier records often stopped at "the message arrived", which is exactly how this gap was hidden.

The file contains `textwrap`. This only shows that the text is near line-break or indentation handling, not what the specific formatting rules are. If a label line displays abnormally, first save the display fragment after line-break handling separately from the label values themselves. When label values contain commas, spaces, or multiple lines, be especially careful not to change the finding just to make a screenshot look tidy; first check whether the original set and the displayed line are already at different content layers.

The old example treated labels as supplementary notes and simply skipped over them once the body could be displayed. That habit later became inappropriate: for users of Slack-compatible Webhook, labels are part of the visible text in a notification. After migration, they should be checked as a separate display item, rather than tacked onto "the notification can be delivered" and counted as checked in passing.

One other step from the old process can be retained: preserve the finding as-is first, then troubleshoot the display text. This avoids repeatedly modifying the source object to try to match a particular screenshot when the receiver displays something abnormally. It also prevents changes in label content from being mistaken for changes in line breaks.

## How Request Waiting Was Previously Assessed

There has always been less documentation for Slack API Request Timeouts than for labels. Initially, some people took "the same notification was received" as indirect evidence that the request had not timed out. This claim was later revised: at most, it shows that the request path eventually returned a response on that occasion, not which wait limit was used during the request, nor that another call would behave the same way.

When migrating out of the old path, the record for the occurrence only needs to keep a few facts together: the parameter order still available when the request was triggered, the actual return status, or the original exception text if there was no response; also note whether this call used the Slack-compatible Webhook path or the Slack API path. Whether the label text was visible can be another observation from the same occurrence, but it cannot be used to explain request waiting.

Do not infer a specific wait value from the import of `requests`. The import only helps locate the area around sending; it does not record the parameters of that request, nor does it replace the actual return status. The old version presented "no need to retain a request record after sending succeeds" as a simplified step, and that passage should now be treated as outdated. It has not been deleted because some people still follow it to confirm reachability when returning to the old troubleshooting process; but when the issue is request waiting, the return status must be retained separately.

There is currently no complete, reusable sample from a timeout incident. Therefore, there are no fixed parameters here, and a seemingly stable default should not be added. If an actual trigger occurs later, first retain the parameter order and return status from that call; if the only information is "very slow", it remains only an incomplete lead.

## Transition Approach for Callers Requiring Compatibility

During compatibility sign-off, not all legacy callers are required to switch to the new record format at the same time. Those still using the old checks can continue to retain the original send results, then add a copy of the label text or a request record depending on what can be captured in each case. This is not intended to keep the two processes running in parallel long-term, but to avoid losing both the old reachability clues and the new text boundaries in a single migration.

You can first handle use cases where the label display is consistently visible, then handle use cases where request waiting actually occurs. This order is only the order for collecting material, not an indication that the implementation has already been split into two sinks. The common entry point that can currently be confirmed is still the webhook sink; no finer-grained attribution of calls can be inferred from this old record.

If a caller can only provide a screenshot from the receiver, migrate the label record first and leave the timeout field blank. If a caller only retained the request result, migrate the timeout record first and leave the label field blank. Do not fill the gaps with another notification just to complete the same table. Such records from actual runs are incomplete, but they preserve differences better than marking every gap as "delivered".

A more aggressive approach was initially proposed: first standardize the text format, then standardize the wait parameters, and finally replace the old troubleshooting instructions all at once. This approach was not pursued further. At the time, there was not enough evidence from actual runs to separate the effects of the two changes, and a direct replacement would have made both the old reachability clues and the new display checks difficult to trace back. The old instructions were therefore retained, but they are no longer treated as confirmation of label text or request waiting.

## Restoring the Old Path

When the additional recordkeeping affects the pace of troubleshooting, you can temporarily return to the original sending method. When restoring it, retain the original finding and the actual return status after sending. This still answers "did this request complete", and ensures that troubleshooting reached through old links still has a reference point.

Restoring the old method does not mean deleting differences that have already been observed. If the label text is abnormal, retain the anomaly together with the old send result; if a request did not return, do not overwrite that record just because a later send succeeds. The old path is suitable for restoring reachability checks, not for erasing differences observed in actual runs.

There was also another recovery practice in the past: first delete the text-related records, then have the receiver confirm whether messages were arriving again. It helped quickly determine whether sending had recovered, but it pushed label issues back into guesswork based on screenshots. It is retained here as historical context and is no longer recommended as the default action. Restore the sending method, rather than also discarding the known display boundaries.

## Gaps Left at the Bottom of the Page

- There is no reusable Slack API Request Timeouts incident record, so fixed wait parameters cannot be specified here.
- The current entry point shows the adjacency between `requests` and the report block; finer branches of text assembly still need to be checked separately in the corresponding revision.
- For the display differences on the Slack-compatible receiver, the available material is insufficient to determine whether they are caused by the payload text, the receiver's interpretation, or both.

This page later served mainly as a way to find the webhook path again through old issue names. For runtime parameters or the return status from a particular run, you still need to return to the evidence from that run; what is retained here is why the old checks were split apart, and the boundaries that must no longer be confused when restoring the old sending method.

# Chart Title and Legend History

Originally, this page placed the chart title template and the legend toggle in the same pending item. That wording came from the starting point for investigation at the time: when a chart in a report changed, both the title and the legend would be noticed first. It did not state that the two shared parameters, nor did it describe the default behavior of either object. The initial draft made only one choice: do not combine two display objects into a single rule just to make the entry look complete.

Later, when the old notes were being organized, ROB-214 required retaining the original dates and pointing to the current entry point, rather than rewriting the earlier text to match the current account. After a capacity review, this item moved into processing; actual work began afterward. These actions on the card only show that the work status changed; they cannot stand in for conclusions about the implementation of title substitution or legend display.

The old paragraphs remain here because they establish a still-useful starting point: if a regression manifests as incorrect chart text, check the title first; if it manifests as missing series descriptions, check the legend first. Both symptoms can occur at the same time, but neither explains the other.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Old notes
    Old notes --> Investigate separately: Title template and legend toggle
    Investigate separately --> Retain old notes: Add findings from actual review
```

The diagram above describes only the order in which the material on this page was handled. It does not indicate a runtime state transition between the title template and the legend toggle, nor does it indicate that chart construction necessarily goes through the same code.

## Options Considered for Retaining the Notes

The first approach was to rewrite the old notes directly using the current wording. This would make them concise to read, but the drawback was also clear: when readers later encountered the paired phrase "title template and legend toggle", they would not be able to tell whether it described a confirmed relationship or a provisional label used at the time to collect issues. This approach was not adopted.

The second approach was to retain an umbrella term and place both objects under "chart display configuration". This would avoid having to classify them, but would obscure the split actually needed during investigation. The source of the title text, the resource context, and template processing form one set of questions; whether the legend appears, where it is passed, and which charts it affects form another. Even if they eventually turn out to be constructed by neighboring code, that proximity should not be described in advance as a single behavior.

The third approach was to retain the old grouping while clearly documenting the locations subsequently confirmed and the remaining gaps. This was the approach adopted. The old text retains its historical context; new addenda cover only objects that have been reviewed, without filling in details for which the initial draft had no supporting material.

| Approach | What is retained | What is given up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overwrite the old notes | A shorter current reading sequence | The original problem boundaries |
| Merge into one master toggle | A single unified name | Separate investigation paths for titles and legends |
| Retain the old notes and add an addendum | Historical judgments and follow-up entry points | The illusion of documenting everything in one pass |

The decision here concerns documentation maintenance, not a ruling on all chart rendering logic. If a new local review confirms only the legend field, add only to the legend section; do not also fill in the complete semantics of the title template. Conversely, confirming one point where a title value is obtained does not prove that the same caller controls the legend.

## Agreed Boundaries for the Record

**Maintain title templates and legend toggles separately.** Subsequent records should be organized around each object. Title-related content should record where the text is obtained, where it may be processed, and which chart object ultimately receives it; legend-related content should record where showing or hiding is triggered and the scope of charts already confirmed. Conclusions about one item must not be extended to the other merely because both appear in the same report.

**Do not rewrite the old notes.** The initial draft's reference to the "same chart area" is no longer used as a basis for combining the two, but remains as the investigation context at the time. Corrections should be added in a separate paragraph that clearly identifies which judgment is being corrected. For example, if it is later discovered that legend control resides further downstream in the report layer, add that finding; do not replace the initial draft's reference to the "same chart area" with a new implementation description.

**Task cards serve only as navigation.** ROB-214 can lead readers to this set of wrap-up materials, but cannot independently prove which placeholders the template supports or the default value of the legend toggle. Card actions, construction parameters in code, and final report output belong to different layers; on this page, only local construction or consumption relationships that have actually been observed may be stated as behavioral conclusions.

**Start the investigation near the chart.** The current entry point is `playbooks/robusta_playbooks/alerts_integration.py`. The chart-related names found there are sufficient as a starting point for searching, but not sufficient to establish that all report rendering logic belongs to this file. Continue following construction and data passing, rather than inferring compatibility scope directly from filenames, function names, or import names.

## How to Read the Current Entry Point

At the top of the file, `logging`, `re`, `time`, and `defaultdict` are visible. These direct dependencies only show that the file handles several adjacent responsibilities. The presence of `re` must not be taken to mean that title templates are necessarily processed using regular expressions, nor must the presence of `defaultdict` be taken to mean that legend data is necessarily aggregated here.

When investigating, first locate `create_graph_enrichment`. What needs to be confirmed here is where the chart enrichment object is created or handed off, rather than assuming the meaning of its parameters in advance. Next, inspect the call sites of `custom_graph_enricher` and distinguish whether the caller passes resource context, title text, or other display options. If the call does not hold a particular piece of information, record that accurately as well, rather than filling in the missing information as a default value.

The source of each assignment to `graph_title` should be recorded separately. A title ultimately looking like a resource name does not establish that the resource name is part of the template substitution rules; it may be text assembled in advance by the caller, or it may simply be the result of a particular branch. `namespace`, `resource`, and `name` are likewise only names near this entry point that require further confirmation. They may participate in resource lookup, title construction, or other context; the existing material has not established the roles of these three names.

Finally, inspect the handoff point for `graph`. The focus is not on finding a variable name that looks like a legend, but on confirming whether legend control is carried on the chart object, handled in the report block, or determined by a caller further downstream. These three locations have different compatibility implications: changes to an object field may propagate with the object; report-layer handling may affect only a particular type of output; caller parameters must not be directly described as default behavior.

This reading order retains a necessary constraint: adjacent names do not imply connected calls. Only after observing the actual passing of data between the construction point and the consumption point may title text, resource context, and legend control be described as parts of the same chain.

## Do Not Substitute One Type of Issue for the Other

Reviewing title templates requires distinguishing at least three levels. The first is the point where the template text gets its value: whether it is provided by the caller or selected during chart construction. The second is which fragments of the text are actually processed: literal text, candidate placeholder fragments, and unrecognized fragments should not be lumped together as "successful substitution" or "failed substitution". The third is the resource context available during processing. One chart lacking a particular piece of context does not prove that all title templates are ineffective; one chart displaying correctly does not prove that all resource types follow the same path.

A legend review likewise cannot be reduced to just two outcomes, "shown" or "hidden". First establish where the toggle resides, then record the scope of objects it affects. If subsequent investigation finds only a value passed by one caller, that is merely that caller's choice and is not sufficient to establish a default value. If only a particular type of chart is confirmed to be affected, that conclusion must not be extended to the entire report either.

The only established point of overlap between titles and legends is that both affect the chart the reader sees. The title can change while the legend remains unchanged; the legend can be hidden while the title text remains exactly as it was. Future regression records should first select one of these objects, then record whether the other changes at the same time. When a shared parameter is found, add that specific connection.

## Retained Earlier Judgments and Later Addenda

The initial draft treated the "same chart area" as a reason to combine the records. That judgment is no longer used. More precisely: the same chart area is only a starting point for investigation, not a basis for attributing behavior. It is retained to explain why this page evolved from one broad to-do item into two objects to be investigated separately.

The names listed in the initial draft remain useful, but their purpose is narrowed to navigation. `graph` points to the vicinity of the chart object; `custom_graph_enricher` points to the custom enrichment call; `create_graph_enrichment` points to the construction handoff; `namespace`, `resource`, `name`, and `graph_title` indicate that investigation should continue into where the data enters. They are not a list of supported template features or a public interface commitment.

The next update should prioritize filling in these points: the direct source of the title text; whether `graph_title` changes before and after construction; whether `custom_graph_enricher` receives resource context; the actual field location of the legend toggle; and whether the two have any confirmed shared parameters. DOC-23 deal with multi-resource selectors, event filtering, and scan event delivery, and are not included in this page's conclusions about chart display.

# Multi-resource event delivery proposal

This compatibility wrap-up reviews multi-resource selectors, event filtering, and scan-event delivery to subscribers together because callers go through both resource checks and the event output path; this does not mean the two should be implemented at the same layer.

The proposal is to keep two boundaries to start with. Selectors organize resource types and operation conditions into comparable input, and filtering uses only that input to decide whether processing should continue. Scan-event delivery is only responsible for passing already-formed events to subscribers and must not reinterpret resource conditions during delivery. This lets callers finish filtering before subscribing and also leaves room to retain unfiltered scan-event subscriptions later.

The shortest path is to check the existing event objects starting with `src/robusta/integrations/kubernetes/autogenerated/events.py`, then decide where the interface belongs. The file header shows dependencies on `dataclass`, `abstractmethod`, `logging`, and `traceback`, indicating that both data objects and abstraction boundaries are present here, at a minimum; at this point, we should not put all selector logic here based on the filename alone.

There are two options:

- Add multi-resource conditions alongside the event objects, with callers filtering before dispatch; this keeps the changes localized, but gives the event layer more knowledge of resource semantics.
- Keep condition matching on the trigger side, with event objects carrying only the resource and operation; this gives a cleaner boundary, but subscribers that need the same filtering will need another integration point.

Start with one round of examples using the second option. What needs to be confirmed is not "whether events can be emitted", but whether callers can explain which condition excluded an event when multiple resource conditions are present at once. If the filtering result cannot retain that distinction, revert to an entry point that supports only a single resource condition. The scan-event subscription interface makes no commitments yet on replay, ordering, or retries on failure.

# Multi-Resource Event Delivery Proposal

The previous version grouped the multi-resource selector, event filtering, and scan event subscriptions into the same round of discussion so that the two entry points visible to callers could first be discussed together. After review, this documentation structure is retained, but it is not treated as an implementation breakdown: when resource conditions go wrong, the first thing to establish is why the event did not proceed; when subscription delivery goes wrong, the first thing to establish is which handler received the event that had already been created. Both problems can occur for the same caller, but their troubleshooting materials should not be mixed together.

This version is the interface proposal from that time, retained for those still revisiting the compatibility wrap-up. It does not claim that the existing call chains have completed migration, nor does it extend the delivery constraints for scan events to all Kubernetes events. The earlier description that interpreted the filename directly as the "event delivery layer" went too far; below, this discussion is instead documented in terms of visible objects, candidate implementation locations, and withdrawal conditions.

## Starting Point and Verification Locations

The review still starts with `src/robusta/integrations/kubernetes/autogenerated/events.py`. The file header directly shows `logging`, `traceback`, `dataclass`, and `abstractmethod`. This makes it a suitable starting point close to event objects and abstraction boundaries: data shapes, exception logging, and abstract methods are likely to meet here. This is not enough to establish that filters, dispatchers, and subscription handlers are necessarily implemented in this file, much less to place resource matching on the side responsible for automatically generating event objects based on this location alone.

Earlier troubleshooting notes pointed to this path through issue names and call names. This navigation is retained so that later readers can first check the event declarations in the same revision, then decide whether to continue following references. The interface proposal does not use path location as a substitute for call relationships. The discussion still concerns two local issues: how multi-resource conditions are evaluated before subsequent processing, and how scan events are passed to subscribers after they have been created.

The starting point at the time was simple: a trigger needs to express multiple candidate resources, but this need should not force the event object itself to be split into a set of new types. Resource kinds and operation names were to be normalized to lowercase before matching. That way, inputs with the same meaning would not produce different results because callers retained different capitalization. This normalization serves only comparison; it does not amount to inventing new resource semantics for events.

## Proposed Two-Stage Flow

The selector stage takes a resource list and an operation list, prepares the input, then determines whether processing should continue. The filtering stage occurs before subscription handlers: events that do not satisfy the resource and operation conditions do not enter subscription callbacks; PubSub does not repeat the resource check at delivery time either. This keeps filtering logic concentrated near the trigger, while subscribers handle only events already permitted for delivery.

Another approach was considered at the time: dispatch the complete event to each subscriber first, then let subscribers filter it themselves. Its advantage is one fewer conditional check in the central layer, while subscribers can retain differences according to their own needs. The problem is that different subscribers may keep or discard the same event based on different conditions; the dispatch side cannot explain why a particular resource received no further processing. For cases such as ROB-218, where outputs cannot be consistently reproduced, this would push troubleshooting back to each caller. For that reason, "subscribers filter for themselves" was not adopted as the default proposal.

Another candidate was to attach multi-resource conditions directly at the point where event objects are created, and dispatch only after a match. The call chain would be shorter, and resource inputs would be closer to filtering results; the cost is that the event creation point would start to understand trigger conditions. The contrasting approach is to let event objects retain the resource, operation, and event name, have a dedicated trigger adapter layer perform matching, and then call the subscription interface. The latter adds an adaptation point but does not require scan event objects to take on selector responsibilities.

This round favors the second approach. It allows scan events to retain a general event shape and leaves room to add subscribers for non-scan events later. This preference does not mean that the adapter layer's file location has already been decided; it only makes sense if that layer can reliably obtain the resource kind, operation, and original event name. If the adapter layer receives only a flattened payload, it cannot reliably reconstruct the comparison inputs the selector needs.

## Scope of the Subscription Interface

The proposed name for the scan event subscription interface is `EventsPubSub`. It allows subscription handlers to register and dispatches the event name and keyword arguments to subscribers. Both must be included in the same dispatch: passing only the resource object would deprive scan-related callers of the basis for branching by event name; passing only the event name would lose the context handlers need to continue processing.

This layer is responsible only for delivering events that have already been created. It does not reinterpret resource conditions, nor does this proposal promise event replay, global ordering, or retries after a subscription handler fails. Adding all these capabilities to the interface would turn the minimal delivery entry point originally intended for scan events into another set of queue semantics, and there was no supporting material for such an expansion at the time.

Whether dispatch continues when a subscription handler throws an exception was one item left unresolved in the review. If it continues, subsequent subscribers may still receive the event, but the earlier handler's failure needs a traceable record; if it stops, a single subscriber will block subsequent processing. Neither behavior can be inferred directly from the existing dependencies in the file header or the interface name, so this version makes no decision on it.

## Verification Using ROB-218 and ROB-220

ROB-218 records that the output of Multi-Resource Selector and Filter Events could not be consistently reproduced. Verification examples should not record only "event present" or "event absent" outcomes. For the same input, they must at least distinguish between a resource-kind mismatch, an operation mismatch, and a case where one of several conditions matches but another does not. Only then can the issue be identified as input normalization, condition combination, or filtering before the event reaches the subscription. If all that remains on the dispatch side is a Boolean result, callers still cannot explain which part of the conditions caused the exclusion.

The semantics for combining resource conditions have not yet been decided. The name "multi-resource" cannot determine whether matching any one of multiple resource conditions is enough to proceed, or whether all must be satisfied. These two choices directly change the outcome of partial matches in the ROB-218 examples and also affect whether filtering reasons can be explained. Until this is confirmed, neither kind of combined result is to be stated as a compatibility guarantee.

ROB-220 investigates the actual entry point for scan event PubSub. It calls for finding callers still using this delivery mechanism and checking their actual versions, entry points, and current results. The investigation should first confirm whether subscription handlers receive the event name and keyword arguments, then determine whether the caller has integrated a selector before subscription. A single successful subscription cannot be used to infer that all scan events pass through the same dispatcher, nor can an independent filtering boundary be dismissed because one caller does not use filtering.

One related issue remains under DOC-24: Finding and namespace Label scope. Resource-kind and operation conditions address only resource matching and are not sufficient to replace a label-scope check. Folding label scope into this proposal would make "resource mismatch" and "label scope mismatch" appear as the same kind of filtering in the output, and would also make the reproduction results for ROB-218 indistinguishable.

## Withdrawal Conditions

If multiple resource conditions cannot produce stable, explainable filtering results within the same call, first withdraw the multi-resource entry point and retain only the existing single-resource condition. This does not reject filtering itself, but avoids exposing callers to results whose originating conditions cannot be identified.

If subscription handlers cannot reliably receive the event name and keyword arguments, do not use PubSub as the default delivery mechanism for scan events, and retain the path where callers handle events directly. Whether to continue dispatching when a handler raises an exception, and whether filtering reasons should be event fields or recorded only on the caller side, also remain unresolved. Until these issues are resolved, this proposal can only be used as review material from that time.

# Notification Rate-Limiting Compatibility Migration Process

This round of migration changes how the compatibility checklist is written. Previously, all notification-related checks tended to end up in one place: some people started from the Pod eviction issue, others from the Sink call name, and what was ultimately left behind was often just "notification path checked". This phrase preserves the search starting point, but cannot show whether what was checked was rate limiting, scope, or time-slice priority.

We are now retaining old records as historical indexes while splitting new records into two tracks. Pod Eviction Notification Rate Limiting records only visible changes before and after notification handling; Sink scope and Time Slice Priority records only one caller that can still be identified. The two tracks may point to the same reading entry, but do not share conclusions.

```text
Old records
Issue name / Call name
        |
        +-- One compatibility checklist
              |
              +-- Notification path checked

After migration
Pod Eviction Notification Rate Limiting
        -> Notification state before trigger
        -> Notification changes after handling

Sink scope and Time Slice Priority
        -> Caller version
        -> Sink entry
        -> Current result
```

## Do Not Clean Up Old Records Yet

The issue names, call names, and paths in old records still have value. When encountering an existing record, first preserve its original wording, and do not rewrite "notification path checked" as an already completed compatibility conclusion. Then note next to the original record which track it belongs to, or state that it cannot yet be classified.

Classification is not based on how many times a term appears. Mentioning pod in a record does not mean it already has a before-and-after comparison of Pod eviction handling; mentioning sink does not mean it already knows the scope through which the caller passed. Only when the original record truly maps to the inputs and results required for this round should it be moved into a new object record. Otherwise, retain it in the old record as a search clue.

An old record may mention both Pod and Sink. In that case, do not rewrite the old sentence or treat the same observation as a completion marker for both sides. You can leave an index position in each of the two new records: fill in the before-and-after notification state on the Pod side, and the version, entry, and current result on the Sink side. This way, later review can still show that both items appeared in the same investigation without concealing information missing from either side.

## When Starting from Pod Eviction Notification Rate Limiting

The starting point for the Pod track is the notification state that was already visible before an eviction-related operation. The record should first state this condition, then state whether handling resulted in additional notifications, fewer notifications, or the same notifications. Without the pre-state, the later "no new additions" cannot distinguish rate-limit suppression from never reaching notification handling.

The second item is the rate-limiting entry point. The entry can be a configuration location, parameter location, or call location that can be located in the inspection at hand; if only the term `rate_limit` is found, still record it as a search term, and do not fill in a window, count, or default value. The checklist needs the actual entry seen this time, not a set of rate-limiting details that merely looks complete.

Post-handling records compare only notification changes. If an extra notification appears, state how it changed relative to before the trigger; if there are no new additions, write only that no new additions were seen this time. Do not generalize from one sample to say that all Pod evictions are suppressed, and especially do not write an observation with no pre-state as rate limiting having taken effect.

Sometimes the processing chain stops before notification handling. This is not the same as "notification was rate-limited". The record for the former should stop at the point where notification handling was not entered; the latter must include a comparable pre-state, processing, and post-state. After migration, keep these two branches separately in the Pod record instead of compressing them into the same "not sent".

If a historical record contains only the eviction object and result, with no pre-handling state, first put it back in the old record, and mark on the Pod track that the missing item is the comparison, rather than adding another generic sink note. The old record can still help the next search start from the same issue name, but it should not carry this round's rate-limiting judgment.

## When Starting from Sink scope and Time Slice Priority

The Sink track starts from the actual caller. Each row must retain at least the caller version, the entry into Sink, and the current result. These three are kept together to prevent combining an entry from one version with a result from another version into a compatibility conclusion.

scope and time-slice priority are recorded separately. scope describes the scope into which this call falls; time-slice priority describes its ordering position in a time-related decision. When both occur for the same caller, write scope first, then the time slice. If the scope has not been confirmed, the time-slice result should not automatically be expanded to other scopes; if only the scope has been confirmed, do not treat the scope as correct as if priority had already been fully checked.

When the caller version is unknown, the entry and result may be left for now, but this row is still a pending item. When the entry is unknown, even if the result looks normal, it cannot be assigned to the current Sink path. When the result is missing, the version and entry are only clues for continuing the check. The goal is not to make every row appear complete, but to make it visible which item is missing.

Same-named Sink callers are not merged automatically. Different versions may retain different entries; different entries may fall under different scopes. When the old record says only "Sink checked", first identify which caller it corresponds to, then decide whether it can enter the new table. If it cannot be identified, retain the wording in the old record; do not use a neighboring module or another caller to fill the blank.

## How to Use the Reading Entry

Historical searches still start from `src/robusta/core/sinks/robusta/dal/supabase_dal.py`. The direct dependencies in the currently visible file header are `json`, `logging`, `threading`, and `time`. These names are useful for helping readers reopen the Python modules viewed at the time and read the data organization, logging, concurrency, and time-related neighbors separately.

In migration records, this path serves only as the reading entry. The Pod track's conclusion still comes from the before-and-after notification comparison; the Sink track's conclusion still comes from the caller version, entry, and current result. Seeing time-related dependencies while reading cannot directly replace the time-slice priority record; seeing the module containing sink cannot replace confirmation of scope.

Old records often end up in this file because the initial investigation began with names and call names such as sink, pod, rate_limit. After migration, you can still continue searching from this starting point, but should switch immediately to the corresponding record track once you find the specific object. This keeps the path while preventing record objects from being mixed again.

## Migration Order

First copy down the original wording and existing search terms from the old record, then create a new object entry. Do not convert the old record to the new format while reading, or it will later be impossible to distinguish the original judgment from the content added this time.

For a Pod entry, first fill in the notification state before the trigger, then the notification change after handling, and only then the rate-limiting entry. If the entry is not found, the before-and-after comparison can still be retained; it simply cannot be attributed to a rate-limiting result. For a Sink entry, first fix the caller version, then write the entry and current result. If the three items come from different inspections, mark them separately rather than merging them into one row marked checked.

When an old record cannot be assigned to either object, continue to keep it under the old record. It may be only a search path, or it may be missing the pre-state, version, or result needed this time. Retaining such records is better than deleting them: the next time the same issue name appears, the search can still be resumed from the original entry.

The minimum sign that migration is complete is not that the old record has been emptied, but that a new entry can answer which object it checked. The Pod entry answers what happened before and after notification handling; the Sink entry answers which caller obtained what result through which entry. Neither type of answer replaces the other.

## Cases for Returning to the Old Path

When the notification state before Pod eviction handling cannot be found, stop writing the notification-change judgment and return to the old record while retaining the search term. If only a rate-limiting-related entry is found but it cannot be connected to the current notification change, do not turn it into a conclusion.

If the Sink caller version is unknown, or the entry and current result were not obtained in the same inspection, stop merging the record. If scope was confirmed on only one side and time-slice priority comes only from the other side, leave the existing content separately; do not present them together as the result for one caller.

Restoring the old path does not involve modifying existing notification settings. It only returns this round's records to the state of "where to continue looking"; after the missing pre-state, version, entry, or result is filled in, classify them again. The record represented by DOC-26 is Slack Investigation Link Toggle, and it is maintained separately from the two migration tracks here.

# Runbook for Failed Release Automation Runs

This page preserves the old on-call guidance written after a failed run. It was written around the release entry point for robusta-release-automation and is useful for preserving the incident state as a first step; it never became a general guide to the release process. When a report comes in, first confirm which run the reporter means. Do not treat a later success after the queue was reordered as the result of the original run.

## First, preserve that run

Open `docs/adj-robusta/runbooks/robusta-release-automation-single-failed-run-on-call-page.md` and locate the run in the release-related records. Record the current revision, its position in the build queue, the artifact versions already shown, and whether the withdrawal window was still open at the time. Here, "current" means the revision shown on the page when the on-call report came in, not a revision from a later resubmission or requeue.

First, capture the state before and after the first anomaly. Do not start by refreshing permissions, retriggering the workflow, replacing artifacts, or clearing failed items from the queue. These actions may get the queue moving, but they can also wipe out both the point where the run originally stalled and the original artifact version. If all that remains is the cleaned-up green state, you cannot use this page to infer that the original failure has recovered. Record it only as "initial result missing."

The old approach used the most recent normal sample as the only baseline. When sampling, keep only one normal run from the same release entry point, and compare only the current revision. At the time, this was considered enough to narrow the issue down to the build queue; that judgment was never fully validated afterward, but it remains here so on-call staff do not mistake it for a confirmed rule.

## Stop at the first difference

Check in the order shown on the page, not according to your guesses:

1. Check whether the release has entered the build queue; if not, record where it stopped at the entry point. Do not start by discussing artifacts.
2. Check whether the queue has started processing that revision; if not, save the queue state before and after it. Do not insert another run ahead of it and then judge whether the original run is usable.
3. Check whether queue processing left an artifact version; if there is no version, keep the first failure recorded at the preceding visible difference. Do not recast "no artifact" as the root cause.
4. If there is an artifact version but it needs to be withdrawn, record the version and window state at the time. Do not overwrite the record with a new artifact of the same name, and do not treat the page after withdrawal as if nothing had ever been released.

Change only one condition at a time. If you retrigger once to check the queue, do not also change the revision or replace the artifact version in the same comparison; otherwise, even if it later turns green, there is no way to tell which step caused the change. This restriction was written at the time to make handoffs easier; it does not mean all release issues can be explained by single-variable comparisons.

Once the first difference appears, stop expanding the scope of your actions. If the queue has not processed the run, you should not continue checking the withdrawal window; if no artifact has been produced, you should not pursue the artifact version as a lead. Conversely, if the queue has processed the run but the artifact records are clearly different, leave the queue state untouched and record the difference and version first. The on-call page only identifies where to stop; it cannot fill in a failure cause that was not observed in the incident.

## Limited actions available on call

You may revisit the release entry point, save the state shown on the page, compare against one normal run, and record the first difference in the handoff notes. Unless this run itself calls for retry validation, do not rerun it. If a rerun is unavoidable, first record the original run and the new run separately; the new run establishes only its own result and cannot overwrite the old run.

For artifacts already within the withdrawal window, first preserve the version and window state, then decide whether to withdraw them. This old page gives withdrawal priority by default because it assumes all anomalies occur after the release queue; that premise is not proven on this page. If the queue has not processed the run, do not withdraw anything under this old guidance. Only preserve the incident state and wait for the maintenance records for the release entry point to be completed.

If the anomaly extends beyond the segment covering `.github/workflows`, the build queue created by release, artifact versions, and the withdrawal window, do not keep trying to fit it into this page's steps. Attach your record of the revision, the first difference, and the actions already taken, and hand it over to the maintainer of the relevant entry point. Adjacent projects retain their own schedules and exit criteria; the on-call page does not declare their runs complete on their behalf.

## Handoff notes

At handoff, leave at least four things: the original run's revision; whether the first difference occurred at the entry point, in the queue, or in the artifact records; what was actually changed for the comparison; and the state of the withdrawal window when checked. Also record hypotheses that have been ruled out, such as "looking only at the revision still doesn't explain the queue position." That way, the next shift won't treat the same hypothesis as a new finding.

Do not replace the first failure with "green later." If someone has already reordered the queue or replaced an artifact, record the original run and subsequent actions separately. If the original state is missing, say so explicitly. Do not fill in the gap by calling it a queue failure, workflow failure, or artifact failure.

## Legacy entry points kept here

This page originally assumed that all failed runs could be traced back starting from the current revision, and prioritized the queue when assigning responsibility. That assumption was never followed up with a recovery drill, nor was it made clear who should take the next step when the queue has processed the run but no artifact has been produced. The page can therefore still be used to preserve the incident state and set stopping points, but should not be used on its own as the basis for a retry, a withdrawal, or ending a release.

If you need to investigate the comparison method further, you can consult the comparison records for the current revision in DOC-30; do not backfill this failed run with the experiment notes from those records.

# Release automation cache trade-off decision

The initial question wasn't which set of results looked tidier, but whether to rebuild the environment before reorganizing the output. The existing setup already had `current revision`, the cache, and the failure exit point; once rebuilt, differences observed afterward could come from the environment, the inputs, and release automation itself at the same time.

The decision is to retain `current revision` without rebuilding the environment at this stage. Keep the cache as reference material, but not as a replacement for the original state; limit the recheck to one real-world usage path, with no changes to the source code or commands as part of this decision.

The alternative is to rebuild first, then replace the old results with the new ones. We are not adopting it yet: the material on hand isn't enough to disentangle the changes between the pre- and post-rebuild states.

# Release automation cache trade-off decision

This record captures a limited trade-off. When the discussion began, the existing release automation setup was not clean: the cache contained organized results, while the original state retained the inputs, commands, `current revision`, and failure exit point. The two are not interchangeable. The cache is useful for comparing artifacts that have already been organized; the original state preserves the clues to why things stopped at that point.

Two options remained after review:

| Approach | What it provides | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild the environment, then organize the results | A newly generated set of results | The version and failure exit point from the original state would no longer be in the same record as the new results |
| Retain `current revision` and recheck just one path | Local results can be compared before and after one environment change | The sample is narrow and cannot represent the entire build queue |

We chose the second row. Preserving the state here does not mean freezing all subsequent work; it means fixing the comparison baseline: leave the source code and commands unchanged, rerun in another environment, and keep `current revision` alongside the results. This lets us discuss environment changes; if the inputs change too, subsequent output will have no comparable starting point.

The objections have not been withdrawn. A rerun in a single environment only establishes that this one path has been rechecked; it does not show that other artifact versions or other build paths are also free of problems. Nor was rebuilding the environment deemed wrong; it can be discussed once the original state has been fully preserved and results genuinely need to be regenerated. We did not choose it this time because rebuilding first would introduce an additional variable that cannot be isolated.

Later cards broke the decision down into concrete actions. ROBA-001 document failure reproduction in a single environment: keep the source code and commands unchanged, rerun in another environment, and save `current revision` alongside the results. ROBA-004 require saving the exit code, `robusta · Release Automation`, and the final log segment before release. The former is for comparison, and the latter preserves the context at exit; keeping only a cache summary does not count as completing both.

When the revisions on the two sides differ, ROBA-011 first hold the inputs for "robusta-release-automation cache vs. original state trade-off" fixed and compare only the two revisions. ROBA-014 stop their comparison even earlier: compare the generation commands and times on both sides, then stop at the first divergence. This avoids recording cascading changes after the first difference as multiple independent issues.

Rollback is no longer recorded as a single blanket status either. ROBA-008 call for checking the rollback entry point and the exit action separately; the old entry point can still be used for comparison, but that does not mean the exit action has restored all state. Partial recovery cannot be recorded as fully complete on that basis.

The decision remains to preserve the original state and use the cache as a supplementary reference, without rebuilding the environment in this round just to organize the results. Expand the scope of comparison only when new real-world usage paths emerge; each added path needs its own commands, revision, and exit-related records.

# Decision on Cache Trade-offs in Release Automation

When this record was first written, the run state was already split into two parts: cached results that could be reviewed repeatedly, and the original state from the run at the time. The former was more convenient, while the latter was less tidy but still retained the inputs, commands, `current revision`, and failure exit point. The question was not whether the cache could be used, but whether the entire environment should be rebuilt before organizing the output.

The brief conclusion at the time was to retain `current revision` and not rebuild the environment. This conclusion only addressed how to make the immediate comparison; it did not declare that all release automation paths had been rechecked. Initially, the paths currently in use in the build queue had not yet been clearly listed, nor had the relationship between the backout entry point and the exit action been clarified, so that version was not expanded further.

Later, someone suggested simply rebuilding the environment and replacing the original run state with the newly produced results. This suggestion is retained here, not adopted as the current practice. A rebuild can produce tidier artifacts, but it also replaces the environment and may separate the original inputs and failure exit point from the new results. If the source code, commands, environment, and cache all change together, even if one run succeeds later, it is hard to say exactly which item changed the result.

Thus, the current decision is not "the cache is better than the original run state", but to save the original run state first and then let the cache serve the comparison role it is suited to. The cache can help show output that has already been organized; it cannot recover exit codes, command context, or the first divergence missing from the original run state. Giving up the original run state first just to get tidy results is too costly in this trade-off.

## Comparison Scope After Review

The review narrowed the candidate approaches to the following two, without discussing a comprehensive rebuild of release automation:

| Approach | Comparison conditions that can be preserved | Main issue |
|---|---|---|
| Rebuild the environment, then organize the results | One set of results in the new environment | There is an additional environment change between the original run state and the new results, and the failure exit point cannot be compared directly |
| Retain the original run state and recheck only one path | The inputs, commands, and `current revision` can be kept in the same record | Covers only one actual path, so the sample is very narrow |

The second approach was chosen. For the recheck, the source code and commands remain unchanged, and the run is simply repeated in an environment on another machine; `current revision` continues to be noted alongside the results. This is not because the other environment is inherently more trustworthy, but to make the environment the only change as far as possible. The results obtained this way are still limited in scope and cannot be used to represent the entire build queue.

The comment that "the sample is too narrow" has not been deleted. It does not reject the decision; it defines the scope boundary: one real usage path can be used to recheck the run state, but it cannot automatically cover artifact versions that have not been encountered, nor can it cover other release paths merely because their names are the same. If a new real path does emerge later, it should be treated as an additional comparison target, rather than having the green or failed result from this comparison copied over to it.

An early version also included the line "organize it later". This sentence is retained as an idea from that time and must not be read retrospectively as a current action. The results can be organized once the original run state has been saved and the differences before and after a rebuild can be explained separately; this is not a prerequisite for releasing the existing run state. This decision prioritizes preserving material that can be revisited, rather than first generating new output that looks uniform.

## How the Run State Was Later Saved in Separate Parts

ROBA-001 established a concrete path for reproducing a failure seen in a single environment: leave the source code and commands unchanged, rerun in an environment on another machine, and save `current revision` alongside the results. This action addresses the comparison conditions. It did not require covering all callers, nor did it present a single rerun as certification of release automation as a whole.

ROBA-004 addresses a different matter: save the exit code, `robusta · Release Automation`, and the final section of the log before releasing the current revision. The exit code indicates the command's exit status; the project name links the output back to the corresponding release automation run state; the final section of the log preserves the context before the run stopped. These three items should not be replaced by a cache summary. Even if the cache contains the final artifact, it may not retain the material from the exit point at the time.

These two cards are easy to conflate because both concern a single run. In fact, ROBA-001 focuses on which conditions to keep unchanged during the rerun, while ROBA-004 focuses on what still needs to be retained before release. The former helps with comparison, and the latter prevents an isolated result from being all that remains after exit. Combining them into "saved and rechecked" would lose this distinction.

Differences in revision are handled separately by ROBA-011. When the robusta-release-automation records on the two sides do not match, first hold the inputs for "robusta-release-automation cache versus original run state trade-off" fixed, then compare the revisions on the two sides. This order is necessary: when the inputs differ, even if the revisions also differ, there is no way to know which side the difference belongs to. This does not assume that either side is the correct version; it simply narrows the comparison to the two sides' revisions under the same inputs.

ROBA-014 moves the stopping point for the investigation even earlier: compare the two sets of generation commands and times, and stop at the first divergence. Many cascading differences may appear after the first divergence, but there is no need to label each one as a separate cause in the same round. Stopping at the earliest difference preserves the later, still-unconfirmed states and avoids hastily rebuilding the environment before the toolchain has been fully checked.

This stopping point does not mean the cause of the failure has been identified. It only indicates how far the comparison can proceed while keeping both sides on the same basis. If further investigation is needed, it should still proceed from the first divergence onward, rather than reconstructing the original run state backward from cached results that have already been organized. The cache can help locate the issue; it does not serve as a substitute for the original commands and times when making judgments.

## A Backout Is Not a Completed State

ROBA-008 exposed another point that is easy to document incorrectly: the rollback entry point and the exit action are not the same thing. Retaining the old entry point means it can still be used as a reference or as an entry point to check during rollback; it does not mean that the exit action has restored all state. On the contrary, the exit action must have its own result, and partial restoration must not be described as full completion.

Therefore, this decision does not present "retaining the old entry point" as evidence of a successful backout. The old entry point, exit code, final section of the log, and revisions on both sides each answer different questions. They can be cross-referenced in the same record, but cannot be compressed into a single generic completion marker. Doing so would leave later readers unable to distinguish whether the entry point still exists, the exit action has been executed, or the records on the two sides match again.

There is also a boundary here that has not been expanded. The rollback check in ROBA-008 only requires checking the entry point and the exit action separately; it does not give a full account of all subsequent states. The current material does not support a backout conclusion covering the entire build queue, so it is still retained as a limited-scope result. If an additional path is included in the backout assessment, a fresh record of that path's own exit material should be kept.

## Alternatives Not Adopted

"Rebuild first, then replace the old results with the new results" has not been deleted, because it may still be useful under a different condition: once the original run state has been saved and build results need to be regenerated, the differences between the new and old environments can be assessed separately. But this is not an action that has been approved for this case. Given the material in this case, rebuilding first would only mix the environment change with the existing divergence.

Another, more aggressive approach would be to treat the organized results in the cache as the sole entry point. This was not adopted either. It would make reading easier but reduce the prominence of the failure exit point and exit material. For this release automation trade-off, being able to return to the original inputs, commands, revision, and first divergence matters more than condensing the results into a single streamlined summary.

This does not require retaining an unlimited amount of material from every run. The current decision only requires that, when comparison or release is needed, the original run state that can explain the differences not be discarded first. The cache remains, and organizing the results can continue; they simply cannot replace the run-state trail already preserved here.

## Current Working Order

The work currently follows this order: first hold the existing inputs fixed, retain `current revision`, and do not rebuild the environment for this comparison; when a recheck is needed, keep the source code and commands unchanged on one real path and change only the environment; before release, save the exit code, `robusta · Release Automation`, and the final section of the log; when the revisions on the two sides do not match, first hold the inputs fixed, then compare the revisions, generation commands, and times, stopping at the first divergence; when a backout occurs, check the rollback entry point and the exit action separately.

This order came from several follow-up notes, rather than from a complete process written at the outset. The initial decision only said not to rebuild the environment, while the later rerun records filled in how to maintain the comparison conditions, the pre-release material filled in what to retain on exit, the comparisons of revisions and command times filled in the stopping point at the divergence, and the backout records filled in the two states that must not be combined.

The remaining limitation is the comparison scope. What the current record establishes is how one path retains its run state, how to avoid treating the cache as the original, and how to avoid presenting partial restoration as full restoration during a backout. Usage paths in the build queue that were not included in this comparison are not considered rechecked merely because they share the same cache name.

When the run state needs to be revisited, the entry point is at `docs/adj-robusta/decisions/robusta-release-automation-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoffs.md`. ROBA-001, ROBA-004, ROBA-008, ROBA-011, and ROBA-014 retain limited-scope records of the single-environment rerun, pre-release output, backout separation, revision comparison, and first divergence, respectively.

# Documentation Site Cache Trade-off Decision

The documentation site at the current revision retains both the cache entry point and the original state. Both center on helm-documentation-portal, but they answer different questions: the cache remains the entry point for using docs, while the original state preserves the context in which the version notes and handling of expired content occurred. Deleting either one and rebuilding would change the comparison along with the environment.

## Decision Made

This round retains the current revision; we will not rebuild the environment just to obtain a new result. The cache remains the material for the existing entry point, and the original state remains the material for determining why that entry point existed at the time. Both are retained side by side; the cache is not presented as a substitute for the original state, nor is the original state used to claim that the cache can no longer be used.

The other approach considered was to rebuild the environment first, then decide what to retain based on the newly generated documentation site. That would produce a new state, but could not answer where the differences already present between the current cache and the original state came from. The rebuilt result could introduce environmental, generation, and content changes at the same time, causing the original trade-off to lose its point of reference. Therefore, this time we do not treat "getting updated output" as more reliable evidence.

This choice does not mean that the cache has been determined to be permanently correct. The cache may retain an old entry point, and users may misread it as the latest version; the original state may not be suitable as a day-to-day entry point. The counterargument is valid, but it shows that the two kinds of material need to be documented separately, not that they should be immediately conflated. By retaining the current revision, we can at least still see the relationship at the time among the documentation site, version notes, and handling of expired content.

## Scope

The decision covers only the retention order of the cache and the original state. It does not determine whether the docs content has already been updated, nor does it rule out rebuilding the environment as follow-up work. If a rebuild is needed, the material produced by the new environment should be the comparison object for the next round, and must not be backfilled as the original state of the current revision.

An exit action is also not treated as a conclusion in this round. If an exit is carried out later, it should separately record which entry point it changed, what material it retained, and what the result was; without this record, the exit action cannot be used to prove that either the cache or the original state has become invalid.

When a run of `logos-supply-boundary` behaves unexpectedly, first keep together the object entering the boundary audit in this run, the original input, and the first result. ## First, check that the record hasn't been split up

Open `docs/adj-logos/runbooks/logos-dependency-boundary-audit-single-failed-run-on-call-page.md` and find the corresponding execution record. First note the object identifier, its status on entry, and the entry point the page links to; don't restart, refresh permissions, or create another run as a substitute for the original state. If the entry point has switched to another project, record only that fact; don't bring the other project's results back to this page.

Keep successive statuses for the same object in the order they appeared. If a status change looks like two objects, go back to the object identifiers and check them first; don't merge objects just because their names are similar, or delete earlier records just because only the later status remains. `ROBD-004` retains links for checking the two statuses of the same `logos-supply-boundary` object. This page originally said only "Stop at the first failure." Later, a single execution record reported `close` and `timeout` at the same time: keep both statuses, recording where each appeared and their relative order. Don't choose one as the final status or explain away the other as duplicate noise. If you can't confirm whether they belong to the same object, stop at the object check; don't move on to assessing the source.

## Dependency source branches

Once the object is confirmed, check each of the following to see whether this record is still within this project's boundary:

- Continue using the checks on this page only if the record concerns a dependency source established by lock or license.
- The scope of adoption must be traceable to that dependency source. If the scope is unclear, preserve it as recorded; don't change "being adopted" to "already adopted."
- Continue documenting exit actions only if this project still holds exit responsibility. If responsibility has been handed off, is changing, or has no clearly corresponding object, don't make decisions on someone else's behalf.

If any of these three checks can't be confirmed from the record at hand, stop at that check. When you stop, state which has been confirmed: the source, the scope of adoption, or exit responsibility. Don't record unconfirmed items as negative findings, or conclude from a single failure that a particular lock or license is faulty.

If the behavior falls outside these boundaries, retain this project's object and failure location, then hand the compatibility questions that need confirmation over to the public interface side. A caller issue was previously passed to the person responsible for interface compatibility for confirmation; this kind of handoff only means an interface assessment is needed, not that a conclusion has been reached about the dependency source. This project must still retain its own scope of adoption and exit responsibility; don't delete the original run record because the issue has been handed off.

## Stopping, rollback, and reopening

After the first failure, stop any new actions on the current branch first. Don't change the object, dependency source, and exit responsibility at the same time; doing so would make the original failure location impossible to identify. Keep the old entry point, original input, both statuses, and checks already performed during the shift in the record. Any later additions must be appended after the original record.

This page initially overstated a single successful entry-point check. Only later notes separated it back out into three coordination questions. The old wording has not been deleted, because it still explains why the release card was at one point treated as complete prematurely.

The three questions were later separated into three distinct actions: an entry-point result is a limited observation, withdrawal requires maintainer confirmation, and closure is a release status reached after reruns. The old paragraph read:

> If the graph-rendering entry point works, that proves the multi-cluster compatibility regression tests have passed.

An entry point returning the expected result can establish that the observed candidate path works; it cannot, on its own, establish the result for another set of cluster conditions or prove that the old entry point has not regressed. An entry-point check and the full set of regression tests are not the same thing. Having an entry-point result does not mean the full coverage scope has been listed. If the card only includes this result, readers can only confirm that this candidate path was observed; they cannot infer the result for another set of cluster conditions. The latest note did not provide a new, complete scope of coverage, so the partial result is not expanded into an overall conclusion here.

## Who is responsible for withdrawing a candidate path?

Withdrawal of a candidate path is confirmed by that path's maintainer. The person who discovers the issue can record the path, the observed behavior, and the suggested action in the release card, but cannot announce a withdrawal on the maintainer's behalf. If the maintainer has not confirmed it, the page can only say "pending confirmation"; a temporary change on the card must not be recorded as a completed withdrawal, and this page cannot be used to infer a specific person responsible. Until the maintainer confirms, both the candidate path and its withdrawal status must remain on the card. If only the link is deleted, or only the issue reporter's note remains, later readers cannot tell whether the withdrawal actually happened. This is another way the old wording can mislead. The candidate path record and withdrawal confirmation must stay on the same release card to avoid leaving only screenshots or old links behind.

The team continues to use these criteria: the release card may only be closed after someone other than the author has rerun every cumulative chain under the opposite conditions and confirmed that the old entry point has not regressed. The "opposite conditions" here cannot be replaced by a single ordinary successful result; success at the graph-rendering entry point cannot replace this step either.
