# On-Call Handoff Decision Record

First, record the actual action left by the handoff: the existing report-blocks entry point will continue to serve as the fixed starting point for this round of comparison; the window adjustment will not occur at the same time as an entry-point change. This decision does not grant the entry point a long-term pass, nor does it cross the window issue off the handoff record. It addresses only the two change items already considered together in review, and which one should be changed first while the evidence is still not broad enough.

## The Original Question at the Handoff Table

When this started, it did not look like work requiring a redesign of the reporting pipeline. The handoff had an entry point that had already been reviewed, plus a window condition that might affect the observation results. Both could serve as explanations, but they occupy different positions: the entry point determines where the comparison enters report-blocks, while the window determines which conditions are included in the same observation. What is most easily lost in an on-call handoff is precisely the ordering of these two positions.

Kaiheng Cloud framed the issue in review as two actionable paths. The first is to leave the current entry point unchanged and examine the window separately. The second is to change the window first, then decide whether to continue based on the actual conditions. Another seemingly easier approach would be to change the entry point and window together, then work backward from the final result to guess the cause. This third approach was not approved because it cannot show which change caused the difference first.

The documentation requirement in the meeting materials was also narrow: for the same input, change only one condition and record the first observable divergence. It did not require listing every possible input, nor did it provide a fixed value for the window. Accordingly, this page can determine the comparison order and the boundaries of what is retained, but not fill in a value for the actual environment or provide a conclusion covering every path.

## The Brief Note Left by v1

The core sentence actually left by the early version was: "For now, retain the current report-blocks entry point; do not bundle the window adjustment with it." At the time, it also listed the two approaches side by side: retaining the entry point and changing the window. The brief note captured the direction of not changing both at once, but did not clearly distinguish retention from rejection or explain why the first observable divergence was needed.

That brief note still has value. It preserves the narrow scope in which the decision was formed, rather than rewriting an on-call discussion as an overall design for the reporting system. v2 does not remove the ordering it expresses; it only adds the boundaries of the choice: the entry point is a fixed condition, the window is an independent candidate, and a combined change is a rejected combination. That way, people who open the page later will not read "retain the entry point" as "the entry point has been proven correct," nor "put the window on hold" as "the window proposal is no longer valid."

v1 did not provide an actual window value, nor turn a positive or negative scenario into a concrete case. v2 likewise does not add these details. The existing materials only say that the review requires starting with one positive and one negative scenario; they contain no input name, result text, or caller name that can be safely transcribed. This record retains the observation types and does not fabricate samples for the historical record.

## How the Choice Was Narrowed

"Retaining the current entry point" is not a comprehensive evaluation of the old entry point. Its only role in this round is to give the next window comparison an unchanged starting point. If the entry point remains unchanged, the window has a chance to be the only changed condition. If the window instead remains unchanged and only the entry point is rechecked, the same sequence can be used in reverse. What the decision preserves is an identifiable comparison starting point, not permanent priority for any particular object.

"Adjusting the window" was not judged to be a wrong option either. It was retained because the observation results may be related to the window; if the window never changes, there is no way to test this side independently. The reason for deferring it is not that it cannot technically be changed, but that this round does not have enough material to connect a window action with the first divergence point. Once a new run can put the changed item and the first difference in the same record, we can then judge whether the window is worth advancing to the next step.

"Changing the entry point and window together" has an irreparable explanatory gap. If the result does not change, that cannot establish that neither one had an effect; one change may cancel out the other, or the difference may occur at a location that was not recorded. If the result changes, that still cannot directly show whether the entry point or the window was the cause. The final state only tells us that the two observations differ; it cannot replace the intermediate sequence.

Therefore, the review did not accept the proposal to "change them together first and decompose them later." Decomposition is not a statistical action to perform only after the result appears; it is a comparison condition that must be preserved before the run begins. Making one fewer simultaneous change means that we can later return to the same input and reidentify the relationship among the entry point, the window, and the earliest difference.

## Boundaries of the current decision

Four items were approved in this round. First, the current report-blocks entry point remains unchanged until separate entry-point review material is available. Second, the window adjustment remains a candidate and will not be executed together with replacing the entry point. Third, a single comparison may change only one of the entry point or the window; the other must be explicitly recorded as unchanged. Fourth, the record should stop at the earliest observable divergence whenever possible, rather than preserving only the final result.

The scope of these four decisions is established only by the objects that appeared in the handoff review. They do not automatically extend to other entry points, other windows, other calls, or other reporting paths that did not appear. `src/robusta/core/reporting/blocks.py` is the file location examined at the time, and it can help later people return to the objects viewed then; it cannot by itself establish permanent ownership of the entire file, nor can it supply the same decision for objects whose scenarios never appeared.

Likewise, the forward run and the reverse run can each support only their own observations. The forward run can be used to show that the original comparison can reach an observable result, but it cannot prove that all inputs run along the same path. The reverse run can be used to show that at least one point did not occur along the expected path, but the reverse result alone cannot establish that the window or the entry point was the cause. The two types of runs are shown side by side so that one passing record does not become a blanket guarantee, and one failing record does not become the sole attribution.

If the next run produces only a different final report but does not record the earliest intermediate difference, it can at most be noted that the window or entry point merits further inspection; it cannot be written directly as authorization to switch. If there is a clear first difference, we must also determine which condition was actually the only changed item at that time. Both the divergence location and the changed item must be available for retrospective review; if either is missing, the conclusion remains within the current scope.

## Objections were not erased

One view in the review held that, since the entry point has already been carried forward, it should no longer be treated as the default starting point. This concern is about the starting point becoming fixed, not about denying the value of comparison order. The current decision to retain the entry point is only intended to reduce one variable when the window changes alone. If a subsequent run first points the difference to the entry-point side, the entry point can again become the item under adjustment; this page does not grant it an exemption from testing.

Another view held that the window is closer to the observed results, so adjusting the window first would save on-call time. This rationale was retained because it highlighted the practical pressures of handoffs. It was not adopted as the action for this round because "closer" is still not evidence of the first difference. Once the window is changed first, if the entry point also changes in the same case, temporal order cannot be translated into causal order. The review chose to forgo a seemingly faster action in exchange for keeping the comparison interpretable.

There was also concern that once the window was listed as a separate candidate, it would remain pending indefinitely. This concern was not dismissed as insignificant either. The material provides neither a completion time that can be committed to nor results that could replace separate observation, so this page cannot invent a deadline. Retaining the window means giving it a clear place in the next handoff, not claiming that it will definitely be adopted.

These reservations changed the wording but did not overturn the decision. In external communications, writing only "the entry point remains unchanged" could easily be misread as saying that the entry point is correct; writing only "the window is deferred" could easily be misread as saying that the window has been rejected. Both statements must now be tied to the comparison conditions: the entry point is kept unchanged to fix the starting point, the entry point can be rechecked while the window remains unchanged, window adjustments can still be tried separately, and combined changes will not be made.

## The First Observable Divergence

The first observable divergence is not the most prominent change in the final output, nor is it the place that the person handing over considers most likely to be the cause. It refers to the earliest point at which a difference between the two conditions can be observed, following the same input and the recorded comparison sequence. This point must be retained because later results may be affected by multiple steps at once; the further downstream, the harder it is to know what happened earlier.

If the entry point is held constant, only the window changes, and the final results differ, the following questions still need to be answered for that case: where the difference first appeared, whether the entry point really remained unchanged, and whether any other conditions changed at the same time. Without these three points, all that can be said is that the two end results differ, not that a decision to adjust the window has already been reached. Conversely, if the window is held constant and only the entry point is rechecked, the record must also make clear that the window did not change, or the next handoff will bring the window back into the causal explanation.

"No change" also needs to be interpreted carefully. No change after combined changes only shows that this combination left no difference in the end results; it does not prove that both the entry point and the window are irrelevant. No change after changing a single condition likewise only shows that no divergence was observed with the current input and within the current scope of observation; it cannot be generalized to mean that no input will produce a change. The decision requires the scope of observation to be written down, rather than using a single negative term to shut down further checks.

"One positive and one negative case" is not a complete test matrix either. They represent the two directions that the review requires retaining: one shows that the existing comparison can produce observable results, and the other shows that another case did not reach closure as expected. The material does not provide the specifics of either, so this page does not fill in their inputs, outputs, or environments. If subsequent records contain these details, they should be preserved as part of the cases themselves, rather than inferred from the decision sequence on this page.

## Minimum Handoff Record Structure

The handoff does not need to repeat the full background, but it cannot contain only end states such as "window changed" or "results normal". At a minimum, four distinct things must be identifiable: the input used, the conditions held constant, the conditions actually changed, and the earliest point where a difference appeared. If any item was not observed, explicitly state that it was not observed; do not fill the gap with speculation.

| Field | What to record | What this statement cannot stand in for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | The same input actually used in this run | Results from other inputs |
| Fixed item | The entry point or window that remained unchanged | A claim that all unlisted conditions remained unchanged |
| Changed item | The entry point or window adjusted on its own in this run | Attribution after both items are changed together |
| First divergence | The earliest location where a difference is visible | The cause of all subsequent differences |
| Result | The state actually obtained in the current run | Decisions beyond the scope of the run |

This table is not a new review process; it separates terms that are easily conflated during handoffs. If the inputs differ, the two results cannot be combined directly into a single comparison; if the fixed item is not recorded, it is impossible to confirm that only one thing changed; if the first divergence is not recorded, the final result cannot establish the cause. If the run can provide only some of this information, the handoff record should retain only what has already been observed, while also retaining the unanswered items.

For example, if the end of the report changes after the window alone is adjusted, but the first point of divergence has not been located, it is acceptable to write "There is a signal on the window side that warrants further investigation," but not "The window adjustment has been approved." If the first difference clearly appears at a window-related location, it can serve as input to the next decision; it is still necessary to confirm that the entry point did not change at the same time before using this run to judge the window proposal. If a separate recheck of the entry point shows no change, this should not be written up as the entry point never having any effect; all that can be said is that no divergence was observed with the current input.

If the forward and reverse runs did not use the same input, they can still serve as separate local records, but they cannot be presented as a strict controlled comparison. The result of one run cannot supply missing conditions for another. The current materials do not provide input names, window values, or output text, so this page only specifies how the records relate to one another; it does not fill in these details for the person handing off.

## How to use file references

At the time, checks were made by following `src/robusta/core/reporting/blocks.py` and the related call names. The value here is in leaving a file reference that lets people return to the location examined at the time: later readers can see that the review was not a discussion based on abstract names, but involved inspecting objects and call names related to report-blocks. This reference and the decision itself are two different things; they cannot be combined into "The file has already proven the proposal."

Nor should this path be read as the sole entry point for all report-processing logic. The current materials do not list the full call chain or other report objects, nor do they specify where the window conditions are implemented in the file. Therefore, the filename supports revisiting the local objects examined at the time; it does not support expanding this page into a code walkthrough or an overall architecture description.

If a later run still starts from this path, the calls or outputs actually observed should be added to the handoff record for that run, rather than citing this page in place of observation. If the run instead examines another location, the relationship between changes to the entry point and changes to the window must also be made clear. The same path does not mean the same conditions, and the same final result does not mean the same first divergence.

## The approach not adopted

The approach not adopted was not "window adjustment" itself, but combining a window adjustment and an entry point change into a single indivisible action. This appears to save one handoff round trip: change two conditions, wait for the result, and then decide whether to keep them. But this shortcut ties two candidate explanations together. If the result is favorable, there is no way to know which item had an effect; if the result is unfavorable, there is also no way to know which item should be rolled back.

Another formulation that was not adopted was "look at the final result first, then locate the problem after finding one." This would turn issue localization from an observation record into after-the-fact guesswork. If there is a transient divergence in the middle and the endpoint later returns to its original state, the final result may even obscure it completely. The review requires the first observable divergence precisely because a later state does not necessarily preserve an earlier change.

Nor did we adopt the approach of writing the current entry point directly as the final solution. The existing entry point is this round's invariant, not the conclusion of a complete design evaluation. It can continue to serve as the comparison baseline, but this fact does not answer whether it applies to all inputs, all windows, or all paths related to report-blocks. Elevating a fixed condition to a final solution would make the handoff material exceed the evidence currently available.

Likewise, we did not write the window's deferral as a permanent rejection. The window remains on the table; it simply requires an observation that does not involve the entry point. If no such observation is made later, this page will retain only the candidate relationship; if one does occur later, the judgment must be reassessed based on the changed item and the first divergence. The decision does not predetermine an answer for future results.

## What this revision restores

v1 let on-call colleagues know not to change the entry point and the window at the same time, but it did not distinguish between "temporarily retained," "independent candidate," and "combination rejected." v2 preserves the original trade-off, clarifies the scope boundaries of all three, and makes the first observable divergence required by the review part of the decision's execution conditions.

v1 also made "forward and reverse field observations" sound like cases that had already been fully collected. v2 instead records that the review requires retaining these two directions, without filling in specific inputs and results that do not appear in the materials. This preserves the basis for the judgment at the time without disguising details that were not provided as a transcript of an actual observation.

Another change is a clarification of how "no change" should be read. The earlier brief note focused attention on different results, which could lead people to treat the same result as meaning that both changes were ineffective. The current decision separates the endpoint result from the intermediate divergence: no endpoint change does not mean no intermediate change, and an endpoint change does not mean that the cause is already known.

The file path, too, has been pulled back from an easily overinterpreted clue to the role it can actually support. `src/robusta/core/reporting/blocks.py` remains because it is the location of the object checked at the time; this version explicitly does not present it as permanent ownership or as the overall call chain. This narrowing is a revision following this review, not a new judgment about the file's contents.

v2 did not add window values, additional callers, more report paths, or new field cases. The reason is simple: these facts do not appear in the current decision materials. A longer record needs to make the known options, comparison order, failed explanatory approaches, and reservations clear, rather than fill its length with missing engineering details.

## Adjacency relationship with DOC-52

DOC-52 records handoff items for open-source version freezes and switchovers. Both it and this page may be opened during an on-call handoff, but the two pages address different subjects. DOC-51 records how to sequence adjustments to the report-blocks entry point and the window; DOC-52 handles version freezes and switchover handoffs. A version switchover does not automatically change this page's entry-point decision, nor does this page's comparison order supply version-specific evidence for DOC-52.

This reference is only meant to direct readers to neighboring material. Do not combine the two pages into a single causal chain, or include open-source version conditions in the window comparison just because both items appear in a handoff context. When you need to look up switchover details, continue with the records in DOC-52; when you return to this page, still read only the entry point, the window, the single changed item, and the first observable divergence.

## Sentences you can use directly in on-call notes

To avoid overstating conclusions in the handoff, you can use the following sentence patterns, but adapt their content to the actual situation:

- "The entry point remains unchanged, and only the window changes; the first difference has not yet been located."
- "The window remains unchanged, and the entry point is rechecked separately; no divergence has been observed with the current input."
- "The entry point and window change at the same time; the final result has been recorded, but cannot be used to determine which one caused the difference."
- "Evidence from the forward case has been recorded, and the exact location of the reverse-case evidence is still to be added."

These sentences only illustrate the relationships that need to be recorded, and are not instructions to copy empty templates into every handoff. If the actual conditions do not involve the same input, state that explicitly; if anything besides the entry point or window has also changed, you can no longer say "only one condition was changed". If the first difference cannot be located, do not project a downstream change backward and treat it as the cause.

Handoff notes should also distinguish between "observed" and "planning to check". "The window is worth checking separately" is a candidate action, while "the window has already caused the result to change" requires supporting evidence; "the entry point is being held constant for now" is a current condition, while "the entry point is already correct" is a stronger judgment. The two formulations are not interchangeable. This decision retains these distinctions because people taking over after the handoff usually see only the last sentence, and if that sentence is too strong, subsequent comparisons will start from a false premise.

## A sequence to refer back to

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Keep the same input] --> B{Select only one item to change}
    B -->|Window changes| C[Keep the entry point unchanged]
    B -->|Entry point changes| D[Keep the window unchanged]
    B -->|Both change at once| E[Do not adopt, split them apart]
    C --> F[Record the earliest observable divergence]
    D --> F
    F --> G{Can the divergence be located}
    G -->|Yes| H[Continue assessing based only on the corresponding condition]
    G -->|No| I[Keep the current scope]
```

"Keep the entry point unchanged" in the diagram means that no entry point change is introduced during this observation of the window, not that the entry point cannot be reviewed again later. "Keep the window unchanged" means that no window change is introduced during this observation of the entry point, not that the window option has been removed. The two single-change paths can occur in different handoffs, but must not be documented as one mixed path within the same case.

If the divergence is located on the window side, subsequent materials can continue discussing the window option, with the unchanged entry point as an observation condition. If the divergence is located on the entry point side, the window must not be documented as the cause merely because it appears alongside the result. If neither path locates the divergence, the current decision remains in effect: the entry point remains the fixed starting point, the window remains a candidate, and the scope does not expand.

This process does not define the required report format, nor does it prescribe the same comparison method for other projects. It only brings the ordering already adopted in this round of review back into the on-call handoff, preventing "comparison can continue" from being misread as "selection is complete".

## Questions Still Open in the Decision

This page does not resolve exactly what range the window should be adjusted to, nor does it establish which side the first difference will appear on. The current materials contain no window values, no specific callers, and no results from forward or reverse cases that can be transcribed. These are not omitted fields that can be filled in from experience, but information that may only become available in the next observation.

This does not prevent a decision in this round. The decision concerns the order of comparison: when the available cases are insufficient to distinguish the causes, first retain the entry point as the fixed starting point without bundling window changes with entry point changes; the window can still be examined separately. This limited decision is sufficient to constrain the actions in the next handoff, but not to replace the next observation.

If someone later receives only an end result, they should preserve the result itself and note that the first divergence was not located. Do not dress it up as a conclusion about the window or the entry point. If cases from both directions are available, also note whether they use the same input. If the inputs differ, they can still describe local phenomena separately, but cannot serve as the two sides of the same comparison.

If a new case shows that another condition also changed, first correct the comparison conditions in the record, then discuss the result. The second change must not be erased to make the case conform to the decision on this page. If both the window and the entry point really need adjustment, split them into two observations that can be reviewed separately, or acknowledge that this attempt yielded only a combined result and cannot be used to approve either side.

## Current Decision

This round of on-call handoff retains the current report-blocks entry point. Window adjustments remain an option, but must be compared separately from entry point changes. An option that changes both the entry point and the window at once will not be implemented, because it cannot leave a discernible ordering. In the next case, prioritize recording the same input, the sole item changed, and the first observable divergence; without this information, conclusions must remain within the observed scope.

DOC-52 continue to cover the open-source version freeze and switchover handoff, and this page does not incorporate that content. `src/robusta/core/reporting/blocks.py` remains as a local path checked at the time and must not be interpreted as permanent ownership. Retaining an entry point does not mean the entry point is correct, and deferring a window does not mean the window is irrelevant; these two reservations remain in the handoff materials along with the mixed changes that were not adopted.

# Open-Source Version Freeze Cutover Procedure

First enumerate the known consumers of graph-rendering and their old entry points, then decide who will try the candidate path. At this point, only the cutover can be confirmed; the old entry point cannot be deleted first. The candidate path also cannot yet be recorded as completed.

For each consumer, leave a handoff record containing the actual call entry point, the repository version used for the trial, the raw unprocessed results, the rejected hypotheses, and the next owner. The party running the trial must be able to roll back to the old entry point on its own. If either the caller population or the rollback action is missing, the status must continue to read migration in progress.

This handoff form is still missing three specific pieces:

- The consumers of graph-rendering and their respective old entry points;
- Trial participants who can roll back on their own and the recovery action;
- The raw results produced by the trial.

Do not guess consumers from module names yet, and do not use "notified" as a substitute for an entry point. Once the candidate path's location is confirmed, record it alongside the old entry point.

# Open-Source Version Freeze Cutover Procedure

During the open-source version freeze, the cutover for graph-rendering does not start when "the new path is ready"; it starts when the old entry can still be traced back. First count all entry points still in use, then have one consumer that can roll itself back trial the candidate path. The old entry, trial version, and on-site result must be retained together; if any one of them is removed on its own, the person taking over will have great difficulty determining whether what they are seeing is the pre-freeze state, the trial state, or the state after rollback.

This record initially left only three blanks: known consumers, a consumer capable of rollback, and the raw result. Later review did not fill the blanks with speculation; instead, the handoff method was completed into an executable sequence. Continue to process in this sequence: fix the old entry first, register the trial next, and then determine whether recovery is needed. Not all consumers need to switch in the same round, and the fact that one consumer is willing to cooperate does not mean the remaining entries can be migrated together.

## From the Lookup Point Back to the Consumer

The current search starts from `src/robusta/core/reporting/custom_rendering.py` and rendering-related call names. This location is suitable as a trace-back point: it lets the search land near graph-rendering, rather than wandering through directories that may involve reports. It is not a statement of permanent ownership, and it should not be written as though all callers enter from here.

Whenever an actual consumer is found, first record the consumer itself and its direct entry. The entry can be a call site, a call name, or an access method confirmed at the time; do not write only scope terms such as "report side" or "rendering side". If one consumer has two entries, use two rows. Keep entries whose continued use is temporarily unclear in the table as well, with the status set to "Pending verification"; do not delete them just to make the list look cleaner.

Use the following row format for the handoff; spaces do not indicate default values:

```text
Consumer: <actual confirmed object>
Old entry: <call entry or code location>
Repository version: <version used for the trial>
Candidate path: <fill in after on-site confirmation>
Raw result: <original artifact or not obtained>
Working hypothesis: <retain the original wording; if none, not recorded>
Rollback action: <which old entry to restore>
Status: Pending verification / Ready for trial / Trial in progress / Rolled back / Pending review
Next owner: <actual handoff recipient>
```

The repository version must be saved with the trial row; it should not be scattered only across the commit message or verbal handoff. The same candidate path may be tried by different consumers with different versions; if only a generic version label is retained, it will later be impossible to map a piece of raw result back to the entry used at the time. Conversely, a version by itself cannot show that the cutover has been completed: it must appear together with the consumer, old entry, and result.

## Keep the Old Entry Before the Freeze

The old entry has two purposes in this work. First, it lets consumers that have not yet been trialed continue running through the existing access method, without being pulled into another consumer's experiment. Second, it is the rollback landing point. If the candidate path behaves abnormally, the recovery action is not a description such as "roll back a bit"; it is a return to the old entry already written in the handoff form.

Therefore, when the candidate path has no concrete location, the old entry cannot be replaced with the phrase "compatibility entry". Do not merge the candidate path and old entry into one name either. They may superficially point to similar rendering logic, but they serve different roles in the handoff record: the old entry is the recovery baseline, and the candidate path is the trial object.

Do not clean up the lookup traces next to the old entry during the freeze. Retaining the actual entry, repository version, and raw result is enough for the next person to continue locating it. Reorganizing these materials into the conclusion "cutover normal" would instead discard clues about where the process entered and at which step it stopped.

## Conditions for Selecting a Trial Consumer

The trial consumer is not just any known consumer. It must at least be able to restore itself to the original entry without waiting for a coordination chain that has not yet been clearly documented. Here, "self-rollback" must be tied to a concrete action target in the record: who is trialing the candidate path, and which old entry is restored after failure. Without this action, even if the consumer has been found, it can only remain in Pending verification or migration in progress.

Do not use "willing to try first" as a substitute for rollback capability. Willingness to cooperate means communication can begin; it does not mean the recovery action is already available. Also do not choose a name first and then reason backward to make it satisfy the conditions; first find a consumer that can recover from the registered entries, then mark it as Ready for trial.

Allow only one such consumer at a time to enter the candidate path. This keeps the raw result from the trial attributable to a clearly identified entry. When multiple consumers switch at the same time, even if the results differ, this handoff record alone cannot determine whether the difference was caused by the candidate path, their respective old entries, or a version difference. The remaining consumers continue using the old entry until their own rows also contain a candidate path and rollback action.

Before the trial, write a complete row instead of filling it in from memory after the trial ends. If the candidate path has not yet been confirmed, leave the status at "Pending verification"; if the raw result has not yet been obtained, explicitly write "Not obtained". These two statuses are more useful than an empty "Migrated", because they show whether the next step is to check the entry or obtain on-site material.

## Raw Results and Old Hypotheses

Keep the raw result in its unprocessed form. It may be output obtained during the trial or a failure symptom observed at the time; if no material was obtained on site, record "Not obtained" rather than writing the absence of a result as no anomaly. An explanatory line may be added beside it, but the explanation must not overwrite the original artifact.

Disproved hypotheses should also remain in the same row or in an adjacent note. For example, if a judgment once attributed the problem to the old entry name and later review found that it was insufficient to explain the situation, retain the old judgment and append the new raw result or observation afterward. Do not silently delete the old hypothesis. Handoffs during an open-source version freeze often have a time gap between two people, and the person who comes later needs to know which statements were merely working assumptions at the time.

The record can be written as follows:

```text
Working hypothesis: The old entry name blocked the cutover (unverified)
Raw result: <retain the content obtained during the trial>
Follow-up handling: The old hypothesis is no longer used as the basis for the cutover; restored to the registered old entry
```

Fill in the follow-up handling only when recovery actually occurred. When recovery has not occurred, do not prewrite it as an established result; when the trial has not yet started, do not fabricate a statement that the "result was normal". Keeping the old hypothesis and new material together makes changes in judgment visible; it is not intended to turn every trial into a complete incident report.

## Cutover and Recovery Flow

```text
Known consumers
    │
    ├── Record the old entry, repository version, and current status
    │
    └── One consumer meeting the self-rollback conditions
              │
              ├── Trial the candidate path and retain the raw result
              │
              └── If a problem occurs, restore the registered old entry
```

This diagram does not mean that the candidate path has become a long-term entry. It only constrains the sequence for this freeze handoff: the candidate path is first handled by one consumer that can recover, and on failure the process returns to the original entry; consumers not participating in the trial do not change status because of the arrows in the diagram.

The recovery action must also be written in the record for the specific consumer, rather than placed in a general explanation. Even when different entries all belong to graph-rendering, their recovery locations may differ. When the handoff shows the status "Rolled back", it should be possible to directly find which old entry it was restored to, which repository version was used, and what raw result was left at the time. If any one of these is missing, the status should remain Pending review.

## Handoff Method After Review

This review continues looking back from the lookup point for `custom_rendering.py`; it does not write the file location as a new sole entry, nor prematurely list unconfirmed consumers as having completed the cutover. The handoff still focuses on retaining four categories side by side: the call entry, repository version, unprocessed raw result, and disproved hypothesis. Together with the next owner, they form the minimum record that can be acted on continuously.

When taking over, first check which row is missing content instead of changing the candidate path first. If the consumer or old entry is missing, continue from the lookup point back to the direct call; if the repository version or raw result is missing, retrieve it from the trial site; if the rollback action is missing, do not let that row enter the trial. The reason for handling it this way is not to require every row to be complete at the same time, but to avoid mixing materials from different stages into a migration that appears to have already been completed.

The caller population and rollback action remain two checkpoints. When the former is unclear, it is impossible to determine whom the trial covered; when the latter is unclear, there is no definite recovery location after failure. Only after both are available should a consumer be marked Ready for trial. Once the trial result returns, decide whether to keep the row on the candidate path, restore the old entry, or move it to Pending review.

DOC-53 records the entry for looking up the upstream dependency upgrade window from sink-routing. Problems in that direction can be routed to DOC-53; this page retains only the freeze cutover, trial, and recovery records for graph-rendering, avoiding the merging of the two lookup paths into a handoff sheet that can no longer be maintained.

# Code-reading notes on the upstream upgrade entry point

When I took over sink-routing, the initial entry point was `src/robusta/core/sinks/pagerduty/pagerduty_sink.py`. This location was noted not because it belonged to the upstream dependency upgrade window, but because the sink's route name showed the next hop during the rerun. First confirm one direct caller; the same-named file has no call edge, so keep it only as a signpost and don't use it to piece together the path.

The receipt from a rerun by someone other than the author was useful: it could distinguish "the names look alike" from "it was actually reached." Continue following the call referenced in the receipt upstream until the upstream dependency upgrade window first actually consumes that result. At that point, you can answer where the entry point is; following other branches inside the sink would only turn this trace into a read-through of PagerDuty's code.

The recorded sequence was deliberately narrow, covering only the public entry point, one direct caller, and the first consumer. If the receipt stops at the caller, it remains marked as not reached; the upgrade window cannot be registered as a consumer on that basis. A matching filename, an adjacent directory, or an incidental import was no substitute for this step.

The trace stopped at a boundary that required an answer from another owner: this rerun did not confirm whether there would be further changes to the routing result after the upgrade window. The old notes therefore identify the first consumer above as the actual entry point, not as the final owner. Anyone using this page to trace the path later should retain this stopping point; it reflects the call relationships at the time, not an assessment of the sink's present ownership.

authoring_topic: A new maintainer starts at the public entry point in sink-routing's repository, follows only one direct caller, then proceeds to the first actual consumer in the upstream dependency upgrade window. Along the way, they use receipts from reruns by someone other than the author as navigation evidence; same-named files without a call edge are only signposts, and they stop at a boundary that requires an answer from another owner.
